title: Nanda's festival in Gokula
hookLine: Vasudeva leaves his son beside sleeping Yashoda, and Gokula welcomes the baby with the birth rite
carry: samskara: sacred rites for life's passages

cards: Gokula is silent. Vasudeva comes up out of the river, soaked, with the baby in his arms, and walks into the cowherd village where his friend Nanda lives. Nobody stops him.
Nobody even stirs. The Bhagavata says everyone in Nanda's household is fast asleep. Inside, Nanda's wife Yashoda has just given birth too.
She lies beside a newborn girl, so deeply asleep that she doesn't know what kind of child she has had.

teach.b: He lays his son beside Yashoda, picks up her daughter, and walks back across the river into the prison. He sets the girl on Devaki's bed.
The text says he put the fetters back on his own feet, and the doors closed, as if nothing had happened. The rescue only works if he locks himself in again.

And the girl he carries is no ordinary child: the Bhagavata has told us she is Yogamaya, the Lord's own power, born to Yashoda for this night. Now Gokula. Yashoda wakes up to a son, and Nanda is overjoyed.
But the first thing he does isn't a party.
He bathes, calls the priests, has the jatakarma done, the birth rite, and honors the gods and his ancestors.
Then the party: he gives away cows and gifts, the village is swept and hung with garlands, and the cowherds splash each other with milk, curd and butter. Here's the teaching.

teach.h: SAMSKARA: SACRED RITES FOR LIFE'S PASSAGES
teach.b: Hindus mark the great passages of a life with sacred rites called samskaras, traditionally counted as sixteen, from before birth to the funeral. A new life isn't only a family's private joy.
It's welcomed before God and the ancestors. That's why some communities keep Nandotsava, Nanda's festival, the day after Janmashtami, with curd and butter.
And it's why, when a baby comes today, a grandmother may want a naming ceremony and a priest, not just a photo. She's doing what Nanda did.

how: Hindus traditionally count sixteen samskaras, rites that mark a life from before birth to the funeral; the birth rite (jatakarma), the naming ceremony (namakarana) and a baby's first rice (annaprashana) are still kept by many families, and some communities keep Nandotsava, the day after Janmashtami, with curd and butter.

games.why: Nandotsava: Nanda had the birth rite done for his son, and the cowherds splashed each other with milk, curd and butter.

practice: Bring to mind a child in your life: a new baby in the family, a niece, a neighbor's little one. In many Hindu homes, when a child bows to an elder, the elder touches the child's head and says, ayushman bhava: may you live long.
Picture that child and say it for them softly, a few times. If you pray, add a name of God you love, the way a family welcomes a newborn before God.
If you don't pray, simply hold that child in steady good wishes: may you live long, may you be well.
